title: India Is About to Witness Its Biggest-Ever IPO Wave — From Jio's $3.8 Billion Listing to Carlsberg's Beer Play
excerpt: Carlsberg has confidentially filed for a $700 million India IPO, joining a pipeline that includes Jio Platforms, NSE, PhonePe, and Pernod Ricard — collectively the largest collection of marquee listings India has ever seen in a single year
body:
India's primary market is about to enter the most consequential stretch in its history. On July 2, Reuters reported that Danish brewer Carlsberg has confidentially filed draft papers for an initial public offering of its Indian unit — a deal that could raise as much as $700 million through a secondary share sale later this year. By itself, that would be a notable event. In the context of the pipeline building behind it, it is merely the latest name on an extraordinary roster.

The second half of 2026 is shaping up to host the biggest concentration of marquee IPOs India has ever seen. The headliners, in order of expected size:

**Jio Platforms — up to $3.8 billion.** Mukesh Ambani's telecom-to-digital conglomerate has begun drafting its initial prospectus, according to Bloomberg. If it lists at the upper end, it would become India's largest-ever IPO, surpassing LIC's ₹21,000 crore offering in 2022. Jio's 490 million subscribers and sprawling digital ecosystem — spanning payments, streaming, retail, and cloud — make it one of the most watched tech listings globally.

**National Stock Exchange (NSE) — potentially $2–3 billion.** India's largest bourse has been working toward a public debut for years, delayed by regulatory investigations that have since been resolved. CEO Ashishkumar Chauhan has indicated the listing could happen in 2026. An NSE IPO would be unique: investors would essentially be buying a piece of the infrastructure that processes nearly 90% of India's equity derivatives volume.

**PhonePe — up to $1.5 billion.** India's largest digital payments platform, backed by Walmart, has confidentially filed for an IPO that could value the fintech firm at roughly $15 billion. PhonePe processes over 50% of all UPI transactions in India.

**Carlsberg India — up to $700 million.** The second-largest brewer in India (22% market share, behind Kingfisher's United Breweries) operates 14 breweries and is betting on India's fast-growing young-adult alcohol market. Kotak Mahindra Capital, JPMorgan, and Citigroup are advising.

**Pernod Ricard India — size undisclosed.** The maker of Absolut vodka and Chivas Regal is separately exploring a listing of its Indian business, which dominates the premium spirits segment.



> **"**Earnings visibility.** As Ninghui Liu of State Street put it: "India is not a low-growth or broken story, but it is a market where valuations remain relatively full."**


And those are just the headline acts. Coca-Cola's Indian bottling unit (Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages, potentially $1 billion), quick-commerce platform Zepto ($500 million filed), and SBI Funds Management ($1.2 billion) are all in various stages of preparation.

## Why Now?

Three forces are converging.


![Ashishkumar Chauhan — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/09/Ashish_Chauhan_at_the_World_Economic_Forum_on_India_2012_%28cropped%29.jpg)


First, **valuations have reset.** Indian stock valuations have fallen back near their five-year average, with their premium over global peers at a four-year low. For companies that delayed listing during the frothy 2024–25 era, the current environment offers a more sustainable entry point — and less risk of an embarrassing post-listing slide.

Second, **foreign money is flowing back.** Global funds pulled billions from Indian equities during the oil shock and rupee crisis of early 2026. But with Brent crude now below $72 (down 43% from the Iran-war peak of $126), the rupee recovering to 94.50 from its 97 low, and India's banking system at its healthiest in a generation, portfolio managers from M&G to Eastspring are rebuilding positions. That inflow creates the buy-side appetite mega-IPOs need.

Third, **the regulatory pipeline is clearing.** SEBI has been accelerating IPO approvals, and the NSE's long-standing regulatory overhang has been resolved. The infrastructure for large offerings — including the GIFT City route that allows NRI participation — is more mature than ever.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

For diaspora investors, this pipeline presents both opportunity and risk.

**Access.** NRIs with active demat accounts (through banks like ICICI, HDFC, or SBI) can apply for IPOs directly. Those without can route investments through GIFT City–based international exchanges. Retail allotments in large IPOs tend to be oversubscribed, so allocation is never guaranteed — but the sheer number of offerings increases the odds of securing shares in at least some.

**Absorption risk.** The elephant in the room is whether India's market can digest this much issuance simultaneously. In 2024, India raised a record ₹1.96 trillion through 91 mainboard IPOs; in 2025, ₹1.76 trillion across 103 issues. But 2026 activity has cooled — just 23 IPOs raising ₹21,506 crore so far — partly because of the geopolitical volatility. Stacking Jio, NSE, PhonePe, and Carlsberg into the same six-month window could strain market liquidity, especially if global risk appetite sours again.

**Sector concentration.** The pipeline is heavy on consumer brands (Carlsberg, Pernod Ricard, Coca-Cola India) and digital platforms (Jio, PhonePe, Zepto). Investors will need to weigh whether these premium valuations are justified by growth, or whether they are paying for hype in a market that has already rotated toward industrials and manufacturing.

**Earnings visibility.** As Ninghui Liu of State Street put it: "India is not a low-growth or broken story, but it is a market where valuations remain relatively full. The bar for increasing allocation is quite clear: we need to see sustained earnings recovery coming through." MSCI India members are projected to grow earnings 15.9% in 2026, up from just 2% last year — but that acceleration needs to materialise, not just be forecast.

## The Bottom Line

The second half of 2026 could redefine India's capital markets. Jio alone would be a landmark; combined with NSE, PhonePe, Carlsberg, and the rest, the pipeline approaches $10 billion in potential issuance. For NRI investors, this is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to own stakes in companies that define modern India's economy — from its digital payments rails to its beer and spirits market.

The risk is that too many marquee names competing for the same pool of capital will dilute returns for all. The reward, if the market holds, is early access to businesses that are structurally positioned for India's next decade of growth. Either way, the second half has begun — and the clock is ticking.
